content: Diarrhoeal diseases are a significant cause of death and illness, particularly among young children in low-income countries. These diseases are closely linked to exposure to human excreta. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions aimed at improving the disposal of human excreta in preventing diarrhoeal diseases. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Disease Group Specialized Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, the metaRegister of Controlled Trials (mRCT), and Chinese-language databases such as Wan Fang and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI-CAJ). Additionally, relevant conference proceedings were manually searched, and researchers and organizations in the field were contacted. References from identified studies were also reviewed. The review included randomized, quasi-randomized, and non-randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared interventions designed to improve the disposal of human excreta with no such interventions. These trials were conducted at the community or household level. Data from eligible studies were extracted, and their methodological quality was assessed according to the protocol. The results were summarized in tables, but due to significant heterogeneity in study designs and intervention types, no pooled statistical effects were calculated. Thirteen studies from six countries, involving over 33,400 participants in rural, urban, and school settings, met the inclusion criteria. In all studies, the interventions were implemented at the community level. While the studies reported varying levels of effectiveness, 11 out of the 13 studies indicated that the interventions provided protection against diarrhoea. However, differences in study populations, settings, baseline sanitation conditions, water and hygiene practices, intervention types, methodologies, compliance levels, and case definitions made it difficult to compare results across studies. Furthermore, the validity of many individual study results was compromised by methodological issues, such as non-random allocation of interventions, insufficient numbers of study clusters, lack of adjustments for clustering, unclear follow-up data, potential reporting bias, and other limitations. The authors concluded that there is some evidence suggesting that interventions to improve the disposal of human excreta can help prevent diarrhoeal diseases. However, this conclusion is primarily based on the consistency of the observed beneficial effects rather than the quality of the evidence. The overall quality of the evidence was poor, and it was not possible to quantify the effectiveness of the interventions. The wide range of reported effects may be attributed to clinical and methodological differences among the studies, as well as variations in exposure levels, intervention types, and biases. To better understand the potential impact of improved excreta disposal on diarrhoea, rigorous studies conducted in diverse settings are needed.
